content: 1. The diagnosis of disseminated tuberculosis (TB) can be supported by various tests, including the Xpert Ultra assay, which is particularly useful for extrapulmonary TB cases. 2. When TB is suspected based on clinical signs and symptoms, a urine sample should be collected for lateral flow lipoarabinomannan (LF-LAM) testing, and a molecular rapid diagnostic test (mWRD) should also be performed. If TB cannot be ruled out, the results of the mWRD should be evaluated, and treatment for TB should be initiated if indicated. 3. If the LF-LAM test result is positive, TB treatment should be started immediately, even while awaiting mWRD results. The LF-LAM result should be interpreted in conjunction with clinical judgment, chest X-ray findings (if available), and any bacteriological results. 4. A negative LF-LAM result does not exclude TB. In such cases, the mWRD results should be evaluated, and further diagnostic evaluations should be conducted as per national guidelines. Additional investigations may include chest X-rays, clinical assessments, or culture testing. 5. If both LF-LAM and mWRD results are negative, or if mWRD is not performed, TB cannot be definitively ruled out. The patient should be re-evaluated, and further testing should be conducted according to national protocols. 6. For patients with HIV who are being evaluated for TB but do not exhibit TB symptoms or are not seriously ill, their CD4 count should be determined. If the CD4 count is less than 100 cells/mm³ or the patient presents with a WHO stage 3 or 4 event, a urine sample should be collected for LF-LAM testing. 7. If the LF-LAM test is positive in HIV patients, TB treatment should be initiated immediately, and additional studies should be conducted to assess drug resistance using rapid molecular methods. 8. If the LF-LAM test is negative in HIV patients, an advanced HIV disease (AHD) package of care should be applied. For patients with CD4 counts between 100–200 cells/mm³, LF-LAM testing is not recommended, and the AHD package of care should be implemented. 9. For patients with CD4 counts greater than 200 cells/mm³ or unknown CD4 counts, LF-LAM testing is not recommended, and clinical management should proceed based on the patient’s condition. 10. The LF-LAM test is designed for use with urine samples and should not be used with other body fluids such as sputum, serum, or cerebrospinal fluid. It does not differentiate between species of the Mycobacterium genus, but in high TB prevalence areas, a positive LF-LAM result is likely attributable to Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC). 11. The LF-LAM test does not replace other diagnostic tests for TB, such as Xpert MTB/RIF, other molecular rapid diagnostic tests, or culture. These tests provide higher diagnostic accuracy and information on drug susceptibility. 12. For patients with rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB) or multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB), drug susceptibility testing (DST) should be conducted before initiating treatment with the preferred shorter all-oral bedaquiline-containing regimen. However, treatment should not be delayed due to the lack of complete DST results. 13. Rapid molecular tests, such as low-complexity automated nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) and second-line line-probe assays (SL-LPAs), are recommended for detecting resistance to fluoroquinolones (FQs) and other drugs. These tests can be performed on sputum or cultured isolates. 14. Phenotypic DST should be conducted for drugs included in the treatment regimen, such as bedaquiline, linezolid, clofazimine, delamanid, and pyrazinamide, using reliable methods in quality-assured laboratories. 15. A shorter all-oral bedaquiline-containing regimen of 9–12 months is the preferred option for eligible MDR/RR-TB patients. This regimen includes bedaquiline, levofloxacin or moxifloxacin, ethionamide, ethambutol, high-dose isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and clofazimine. 16. Individualized longer regimens may be used for MDR/RR-TB patients who do not meet the eligibility criteria for the shorter regimen. Injectable agents such as amikacin should be phased out and replaced with bedaquiline. 17. WHO guidelines emphasize the importance of DST before treatment, particularly for drugs with available molecular rapid diagnostic tests. Rapid molecular tests are available for rifampicin, isoniazid, and fluoroquinolones. 18. A new molecular test for pyrazinamide resistance detection, based on high-complexity reverse hybridization NAAT, is recommended for use with culture isolates. Alternatively, pncA sequencing can be performed when available. 19. Treatment decisions should rely on clinical judgment and all available diagnostic information, including molecular and phenotypic DST results. Treatment should not be delayed while awaiting phenotypic DST results. 20. For patients with high risk or high prevalence of fluoroquinolone resistance, specimens should be referred for culture and phenotypic DST to confirm resistance and guide treatment adjustments.
